learningGoal.source: Explain how terrace building connects land, water and farming, describe how building knowledge links with the way a community is organised, and tell what a landscape shows from the work and rules that keep it going.
learningGoal.back: Explain how building rice terraces connects land, water and rice farming, describe how building knowledge is connected with how a community is organised, and tell apart what a landscape shows and the work and rules that keep it going.

read.sections.0.text.note: Tuwali, Ayangan, Kalanguya = ตูวาลี อายางัน กาลังกูยา (transliterations). Indigenous = ชนพื้นเมือง; cultural landscape = ภูมิทัศน์วัฒนธรรม.
read.sections.0.text.source:
A mountain landscape can contain engineering as well as trees and soil. In Ifugao province, in the northern Philippines, stepped rice fields show how people have shaped slopes for farming. A cultural landscape is a place shaped by the links between people and their surroundings. Ifugao includes different Indigenous communities and languages, among them Tuwali, Ayangan and Kalanguya. Their landscapes and buildings do not stand for every community in the Philippines. Differences between places matter as much as the knowledge they share.

Terrace builders make level pond fields along the curves of the mountain. A terrace is a level field made on a slope. Stone or earth walls hold up the fields, while a network of irrigation carries water from the forest on the heights. Irrigation means bringing water to farmland through a managed system. The shape of the land, the strength of a wall and the movement of water are linked engineering problems. So a terrace's curved outline records decisions about growing food on steep ground. It is not simply a pretty pattern.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A mountain landscape can contain engineering, not only trees and soil. In Ifugao province, in the northern Philippines, stepped rice fields show how people reshaped hillsides for farming. A cultural landscape is a place shaped by the connections between people and their surroundings. Ifugao has several Indigenous groups and languages, among them Tuwali, Ayangan and Kalanguya. Their landscapes and buildings don't stand for every community in the Philippines; the differences between places matter as much as the knowledge they share.

Terrace builders make level flooded fields along the curves of the mountain. A terrace is a field made level on a slope. Stone or earth walls hold the fields up, while an irrigation network brings water from forests higher up. Irrigation means bringing water to farmland through a managed system. The shape of the land, the strength of the walls and the flow of water are linked engineering problems. So a terrace's curved outline records decisions about growing food on steep land, not just a pretty pattern.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Mountains can hold clever building work, not just trees and soil. Ifugao is in the north of the Philippines. There, people shaped steep hills into rice fields. This is a cultural landscape. It is a place shaped by people and nature together. Ifugao has different Indigenous groups. Their languages include Tuwali, Ayangan and Kalanguya. They do not stand for every group in the Philippines.

A terrace is a flat field built on a slope. Builders follow the curve of the mountain. Walls of stone or earth hold each field up. Irrigation brings water to the fields. Here, it comes down from the woods above. The land, the walls and the water all work together. So the curved shapes are not just pretty. They show how people grow food on steep land.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Mountains can contain clever building work, not only trees and soil. Ifugao is in the north of the Philippines. There people turned steep hillsides into rice fields. This is a cultural landscape, a place people and nature made together. Ifugao has several Indigenous groups. Their languages include Tuwali, Ayangan and Kalanguya. They don't stand for every group in the Philippines.

A terrace is a flat field built on a slope. The builders made fields along the curves of the mountain. Stone or earth walls hold up each terrace. Irrigation brings water to the fields. Here water flows down from the forest above. Land, walls and water work together. So these curves aren't just beautiful; they show how people grew food on steep land.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Working together and making a living

read.sections.1.text.source:
The work goes on after the building is done. Fields, walls and water systems need care. UNESCO describes shared upkeep alongside each household owning its own terraces, protected by ancestral rights and customary practices. Customary means guided by a community's established practices and rules. Shared work does not mean that every field belongs to everyone. It means that households depend on links beyond their own plots. Knowledge about planting, protecting the soil and managing water must stay useful across generations.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) describes the wider farming system as linked woodland, fields, villages and water. Small woods above the terraces help control the water that reaches the fields. Rice is only part of people's livelihood, the work and resources through which they meet their needs. Vegetables, fish and other foods also matter, and carving and weaving can bring in money. Customary rules help share out duties towards land, water and woods. The landscape joins practical knowledge, family duties and community decisions. Its survival depends on people earning a living as well as on looking after walls.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Work continues after building is finished. Fields, walls and water systems need care. UNESCO describes shared care alongside each household owning its own terraces, protected by rights inherited from ancestors and customary practice. Customary means following the practices and rules a community has long held. Working together doesn't mean every field belongs to everyone; it means households depend on connections wider than their own land. Knowledge of growing crops, keeping soil and managing water must stay usable from generation to generation.

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) describes the wider farming system as linked forests, fields, villages and water. Small woods above the terraces help control the water flowing down to the fields. Rice is only part of people's livelihood, the work and resources people use to get what they need. Vegetables, fish and other foods matter too, and carving and weaving can bring income. Customary rules help divide duties for caring for land, water and forest. This landscape brings together practical knowledge, family duties and community decisions. Its survival depends on people being able to make a living as much as on caring for the walls.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: FAO kept as Latin letters; the voice will read it as letters. องค์การอาหารและเกษตรแห่งสหประชาชาติ is spelled out in the standard text.
read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The work goes on after building. Walls and water paths need to be fixed. UNESCO says each family owns its own terraces. Their rights come from their ancestors and from customary rules. Customary means following a group's old rules and ways. But families also work as a team to care for the land. Each family needs its neighbours. People pass on what they know about seeds, soil and water.

The FAO is a world group for food and farms. It says the woods, fields, homes and water all link up. Trees above the terraces help control the water. Rice is only part of people's livelihood. A livelihood is how people get what they need. People also grow beans and greens, and eat fish. Carving and weaving bring in money. The group's rules share out the jobs. To keep the landscape, people must be able to earn a living.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Work goes on after building. Walls and waterways need repair. UNESCO says each family owns its own terraces. Their rights come from their ancestors and from customary rules. Customary means following a group's old rules and ways. But families also look after the land together as a team. Each family depends on its neighbours. People pass on knowledge about seeds, soil and water.

FAO is a world organisation for food and farming. FAO says forests, fields, homes and water are all linked. Trees above the terraces help control the water. Rice is only part of people's livelihood. A livelihood is how people get what they need. People also grow beans and vegetables and eat fish. Carving and weaving bring income. The group's rules help share out the work. To keep this landscape, people must be able to make a living.

read.sections.2.text.source:
House building belongs to this wider setting. The National Museum of the Philippines describes an Ayangan house from Mayoyao. It has four hardwood posts, a steep grass roof and timber parts fitted together without iron nails. Its single main room served several household tasks, and rice could be stored in the attic. The shaded space below could be used for activities including community rituals. The museum also describes smaller granaries, or rice stores, beside some houses. These uses connect carpentry, food storage, family life and belief. This house type is one example among the varied building traditions of Ifugao.

Such places are living heritage. The FAO names damage to the environment, and how hard it is to earn enough from farming, as threats to this farming system. A beautiful photograph captures one moment. It cannot show every working link or household decision. So caring for the landscape means supporting the people who use and reshape it, as well as respecting their knowledge. It lasts through choices and work that go on, not because a community stays the same.
read.sections.2.text.back:
House building is part of this wider setting. The National Museum of the Philippines describes an Ayangan house from Mayoyao. It has four hardwood posts, a steep thatched roof and wooden parts fitted together without iron nails. The house's single main room is used for many household tasks, and rice can be stored in the space under the roof. The shaded space under the house can be used for various activities, including community ceremonies. The museum also describes small granaries, or rice stores, beside some houses. These uses connect carpentry, food storage, family life and belief. This kind of house is only one example among Ifugao's varied house-building traditions.

Places like this are living heritage. FAO names environmental damage and the difficulty of earning enough from farming as threats to this farming system. A beautiful photograph captures only one moment and can't show all the connections of each household's work or decisions. So caring for the landscape means supporting the people who use and adapt it, and respecting their knowledge. The landscape lasts because of choices and work that continue, not because the community doesn't change.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Houses are part of this landscape too. The National Museum of the Philippines describes an Ayangan house from Mayoyao. It has four strong wooden posts and a steep grass roof. Its wooden parts fit together without iron nails. One main room was used for many jobs at home. Rice could be stored in the space under the roof. The shady space below could be used for group rituals and other things. Some houses had small rice stores next to them. This is one kind of house. Ifugao has many ways of building.

This is living heritage. The FAO says the land is being harmed. It is also hard to earn enough from farming. A photo shows one moment. It cannot show the work and choices of each family. So caring for this place means helping the people who live and work there. The old ways go on because people keep working and choosing.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Houses are part of this landscape too. The National Museum of the Philippines describes an Ayangan house from Mayoyao. The house has four strong wooden posts and a steep thatched roof. The wooden parts fit together without iron nails. The single main room is used for many household tasks. Rice can be stored under the roof. The shaded space below is used for group ceremonies and other things. Some houses have small rice stores beside them. This is one kind of house; Ifugao has many ways of building houses.

This is living heritage. FAO says the land is being damaged, and earning enough from farming is hard. A photograph shows one moment; it can't show each family's work and choices. So caring for this place means helping the people who live and work there. The old ways go on because people keep working and choosing.

write.example.source: One built thing is the stone or earth wall that holds up each terrace. The reading says these walls and the water channels need care after they are built. Families work together to look after them, but each family owns its own fields. This links with community life because no family can keep its terraces working alone. The photo shows the walls, but not who fixes them.
write.example.back: One built thing is the stone or earth wall that holds up each terrace. The reading says these walls and waterways need care after they are built. Families help each other look after them, but each family owns its own fields. This connects with community life because no family can keep its own terraces working alone. The photograph shows the walls but not who repairs them.

educatorNotes.0.source: A cultural landscape is neither untouched nature nor proof that its communities live the same way or have stopped changing. Shared upkeep does not mean every field is owned by everyone. Ifugao communities do not stand for every community in the Philippines.
educatorNotes.0.back: A cultural landscape is not untouched nature, and not evidence that its communities live the same way or have stopped changing. Shared care doesn't mean every field belongs to everyone. Ifugao communities don't stand for every community in the Philippines.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: retaining walls and level fields linked to food and continuing upkeep; irrigation linked to woodland, water management and cooperation; or the house's attic or granary linked to rice storage and the household's livelihood. Accept other links the reading supports. Learners should not infer ownership, beliefs or a terrace's age from how it looks.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: retaining walls and level fields linked to food and ongoing care; irrigation linked to forests, water management and cooperation; or a house's roof space or granary linked to rice storage and household livelihood. Accept other connections the reading supports. Learners shouldn't infer ownership, beliefs or a terrace's age from its appearance.

educatorNotes.2.source: UNESCO's page for property 722 (retrieved 7 November 2026) supports the place, the engineering, upkeep, ancestral ownership and changing conditions. The lesson does not adopt its "2,000 years" or "virtually unchanged" wording, and the World Heritage listing covers five named clusters, not every rice terrace in the Philippines.
